query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of carbon (0.1 at.%) to a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) can improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in its as-cast or homogenized condition
generation.intervention: Addition of 0.1 at.% carbon to the RHEA
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions, specifically above 700°C, in an oxidizing atmosphere
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of carbides, such as Ta3C and Nb3C, which can act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion
generation.mechanism: The added carbon reacts with the refractory elements in the RHEA to form carbides, which can improve the alloy's resistance to oxidation by reducing the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, as evidenced by a reduced rate of oxidation and a lower loss of material at high temperatures
generation.baseline: The oxidation resistance of the untreated RHEA at high temperatures
generation.boundary: The temperature range above 700°C, where the oxidation resistance of the RHEA is critical
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which the added carbon improves the oxidation resistance of the RHEA, and the optimal amount of carbon to add

falsification_experiment.design: Expose samples of the RHEA with and without the added carbon to high-temperature oxidizing conditions and measure the rate of oxidation and loss of material
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of carbon does not result in a significant improvement in the oxidation resistance of the RHEA, as measured by a reduced rate of oxidation and loss of material, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
